newsitem.title: USA: Wall Street financier fights extradition to Italy.
newsitem.headline: Wall Street financier fights extradition to Italy.

text.p: A federal judge is expected to decide within days whether a jailed Wall Street financier can be released on $10.2 million bail while he fights extradition to Italy.
Felice (Felix) Rovelli, 38, has been jailed in Rhode Island since May 30 on an extradition request by Italian authorities.

In a dramatic, day-long court proceeding on Tuesday, Rovelli's lawyers produced a string of witnesses who vouched for the money manager's integrity and pledged a combined $10.2 million in cash and real estate for his release.
Lawyer Laura Brevetti told the court this would be the largest bond in U.S. history.
Rovelli, an international mutual fund manager frequently quoted in the financial press, is the founder of the Neuberger International Fund, which has 6,500 shareholders and assets of $100 million.
Italian prosecutors suspect $44.6 million paid to three lawyers in 1994 by Rovelli and his mother were bribes that helped his late father win a $653 million court award.
Rovelli, an Italian citizen and permanent U.S. resident, has not lived in Italy since 1976.
He lives in Greenwich, Connecticut, with his American wife and two young children. Rovelli denied any wrongdoing.
Brevetti argued that her client was not a flight risk, and that one of the special circumstances qualifying him for bail was that he was not formally charged with any crime.
Prosecutor John Danaher said Italy's arrest warrant is a charging document under extradition law.
Danaher told Reuters on Wednesday the $10.2 million bail, while seemingly high, is "less than a quarter of the amount he gave away to three lawyers."
In addition to the bail request, Rovelli offered to turn his home into a high-tech detention facility, complete with armed guards.

U.S. Magistrate Judge Thomas P. Smith said he will contemplate whether Rovelli meets the test of "special circumstances," the only condition which makes prisoners facing international extradition eligible for bail.
Rovelli's boss at Neuberger & Berman, Richard Cantor, told the court on Tuesday he personally promised $200,000 towards the bail.
"In an industry which is not necessarily known for good behaviour and warm personal relationships, he (Rovelli) has exhibited all those (qualities)," Cantor said.
Rovelli's friend, Stamford, Connecticut lawyer Charles Grimes, wept on the witness stand as he described Rovelli's loving relationship with his wife and children.
